blocks.text: 1. Ensemble Retrieval

blocks.alt: Retriever A and retriever B combine through fusion into combined results

blocks.text: Ensemble Retrieval names the general pattern behind every combination covered so far: multiple retrieval strategies combined together.
It runs several different retrieval methods at once and merges their combined output, a generalized combination strategy.
2. Naming The Pattern Behind Every Combination
Hybrid Search combined semantic and keyword retrieval; multi-query retrieval combined several phrasings of the same question.
Ensemble retrieval names the general pattern both of those specific combinations already followed.

blocks.text: 3. What Counts As An Ensemble Member

blocks.alt: Dense, sparse, and metadata retrievers are example ensemble members

blocks.text: Any distinct retrieval strategy can serve as one member of the ensemble.
Dense retrieval, sparse retrieval, metadata retrieval, and multi-hop retrieval can all participate together.
4. Independent Retrieval, Then Fusion

blocks.alt: Member 1 and member 2 retrieve independently, then go through fusion

blocks.text: As with reciprocal rank fusion in Hybrid Search, each ensemble member runs its own retrieval independently first.
A fusion step then combines every member's results into one final ranking.
5. Why Diversity Between Members Helps

blocks.alt: Similar members are compared against diverse members

blocks.text: Members that make different kinds of mistakes cover for each other's weaknesses.
Two retrieval methods with identical blind spots add little value combined.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Combining two variants of dense retrieval that share the same blind spot for exact terms adds little value, while combining dense retrieval with sparse retrieval covers two distinct weaknesses at once.

blocks.text: 6. Weighting Ensemble Members

blocks.alt: Member A with weight 0.6 combines with member B with weight 0.4

blocks.text: As with weighting semantic versus keyword signal in Hybrid Search, each ensemble member's results can be weighted differently in the final fusion.
A member that historically performs better can be given more influence over the ranking.
7. Diminishing Benefit Of Adding Members

blocks.alt: Two members are compared against five members with marginal gain

blocks.text: As with diminishing returns with more variations in Multi-Query Retrieval, each additional ensemble member adds less unique coverage than the one before it.
A handful of well chosen, diverse members often outperforms adding many similar ones.

blocks.text: 8. Operational Complexity Of Ensembles
As with the added infrastructure cost in Hybrid Search, every additional ensemble member means another retrieval system to build, run, and maintain.
That operational cost needs to be weighed against the quality gained.
9. Recognizing When Ensemble Retrieval Is Worth The Added Complexity

blocks.alt: A single method being insufficient points toward ensemble retrieval

blocks.text: High stakes systems needing maximum retrieval robustness justify ensemble retrieval.
Simple systems with tight latency budgets may not justify running multiple retrieval strategies.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Combining ensemble members that share the same underlying blind spots, adding little real value.
Adding many similar members instead of a smaller, more diverse set.
Weighting every ensemble member equally without considering their actual historical performance.
Ignoring the operational cost of maintaining multiple retrieval systems in the ensemble.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Ensemble retrieval runs several different retrieval methods at once and merges their combined output.
It names the general pattern that hybrid search and multi-query retrieval already followed.
Any distinct retrieval strategy can serve as one member of the ensemble.
Each member runs its own retrieval independently, then a fusion step combines the results.
Members with different weaknesses cover for each other, making diversity valuable.
Ensemble members can be weighted differently, giving stronger performers more influence.
Each additional member adds less unique coverage than the one before it, showing diminishing returns.
Every additional member means another retrieval system to build, run, and maintain.
